title: Online Linear Programming for Multi-Objective Routing in LLM Serving
technique: Router for decode workers as online LP with time-coupled batch-slot and KV-cache constraints; bid-price control admits a request when its weighted SLO reward exceeds shadow prices; duals tracked by warm-started projected gradient; tail latency decomposed into per-request threshold-indicator rewards

metric_definitions.definition_quote: Let cj denote the period when request j completes (i.e., its final token is processed). The end-to-end latency of request j is cj − tj.
metric_definitions.notes: t_j is the time the request arrives at the router AFTER prefill completes (prefill is done upstream under PD disaggregation), so E2E here excludes prefill; time unit is decode iterations (periods).

metric_definitions.definition_quote: For a tail level x%, the x% tail EEL is the x% quantile of the multiset { cj − tj : j ∈ J }.
metric_definitions.notes: Tail optimized via threshold-indicator rewards, not by direct quantile minimization; weights map to target quantile.

metric_definitions.definition_quote: Let τj denote the period when request j starts decoding, i.e., when ... its first output token is generated. The TTFT of request j is τj − tj.
metric_definitions.notes: Measured from router arrival (post-prefill), so it is effectively router/decode-queue wait plus first decode iteration, NOT the user-visible TTFT including prefill. Under PD mixing (App. A) it includes prefill.

metric_definitions.definition_quote: We do not explicitly report time-per-output-token (TPOT) since TPOT can be recovered as end-to-end latency minus TTFT and normalized by oj .
Let N tok(T) be the total number of decode tokens processed over periods 1, . . . , T across all devices. The (average) token throughput over the horizon is N tok(T)/T.
metric_definitions.notes: Decode tokens only, per period (not per GPU), summed across devices.

slo_spec: No fixed SLO values; operators choose thresholds t′1 (tail E2E) and t′2 (tail TTFT) and weights (α,β,γ,σ,ζ1,ζ2); e.g. weights (0,0,0,0,1,1) for tail emphasis, t′2=49 periods in the tail-weight study.
load_regime: Poisson arrivals, λ=0.4 (stable) and λ=0.5 (mild overload), plus non-stationary 0.4->0.6 shift; ConvSharegpt-like conversational dataset sampled randomly
tradeoff_acknowledged: Weighting average latency (0,1,1,0,0,0) lowers mean EEL/TTFT but can worsen tail metrics 'because the policy is not incentivized to protect the slowest requests'; overload (λ=0.5) deteriorates tails unless tail weights are large.
models: not stated in extracted sections (Vidur profile)
workloads: conversational dataset (Zheng et al., 2023a, LMSYS-style), Poisson arrivals; synthetic prefill/decode ratios 1:4, 4:1 in appendix
extractor_notes: TAIL IN OBJECTIVE: yes, but not as a percentile statistic: the tail terms are indicator rewards 1{latency < t'} (threshold attainment), and the weight zeta indirectly sets the achieved quantile (Fig: 'Tail weights and the achieved tail quantile'). Results table reports P95/P99 EEL. Closest to the user's Vidur RL-routing setting: same simulator, Vidur default baselines (RR, LOR, Random, Power-of-2). Router is decode-side after PD disaggregation, so TTFT/E2E definitions start after prefill. Mean-latency vs tail trade-off shown explicitly.
load_class_quote: For the real dataset, the request arrival process is modeled as a stationary Poisson process, with an arrival rate λ ∈ {0.4, 0.5}.
